status: COMPLETE — §0 through §16 + Defaults table + Source ledger captured in git-1..git-63 (Pro Git book + official git reference docs read in full; no section dropped). sections_accounted maps every section to its rules.
note: Repo-agnostic rule manifest for professional git mastery — the object model, branching, merge vs rebase, interactive rebase, cherry-pick, stash, worktrees, bisect, reflog-based recovery, submodules, hooks, .gitattributes/.gitignore, signed commits/tags, and clean-history hygiene — distilled from the official Pro Git book and git-scm.com/docs reference pages. The .md is authoritative and unchanged; this indexes every actionable rule, typed checkable|judgment|principle, with predicate/reviewer_criterion. Any agent doing git work (branching, rebasing, recovering lost commits, wiring hooks, reviewing history hygiene) applies this manifest. No Genesis-specific APIs.

rules.text: Model git as a content-addressed object store: blobs, trees, and commits are immutable, hashed-by-content objects forming a DAG; branches, tags, HEAD, and the index are just pointers into that DAG. Learn the object model first — every other command in this guide is built from it. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git Objects / Git References.]

Nearly every everyday command is one of exactly two primitive moves: write new object(s), or move a pointer. git reset is the clearest teaching example: up to three trees in strict order — HEAD's branch pointer, then the index, then the working directory — stopping early per --soft/--mixed/--hard. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Reset Demystified.]

Nothing reachable is ever silently gone: a commit survives as long as it's reachable from some ref OR a live reflog entry; git gc only removes what is reachable from neither. This is a time-bounded, local-only safety net, not a backup system. [VERIFIED, git-reflog docs; Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery.]

A blob stores raw file content only — no filename, mode, or path. Identical content anywhere in the repo/history is the SAME blob, referenced by multiple tree entries. Inspect with git cat-file -p; create with git hash-object. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git Objects, 'Object Storage'/'Blob Objects'.]

predicate.spec: a blob object stores only file content (no filename/path/mode) and identical byte content anywhere in the repo hashes to the same blob id.

rules.text: A tree object is one directory level: an ordered list of '<mode> <type> <sha> <name>' entries (type = blob or tree). Build one from the index with git write-tree; read one back with git read-tree [--prefix=<dir>]; inspect with git cat-file -p. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git Objects, 'Tree Objects'.]

predicate.spec: a tree object lists <mode> <type> <sha> <name> entries for exactly one directory level, built via write-tree and readable via cat-file -p / ls-tree.

rules.text: A commit object points to exactly one tree plus zero/one/many parent commits, plus author/committer metadata and a message. Create directly with git commit-tree <tree> [-p <parent>...]. 0 parents = root commit; 2+ parents = merge commit. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git Objects, 'Commit Objects'.]

predicate.spec: a commit object references exactly one tree plus zero-or-more parent commits and author/committer metadata; a commit with 2+ parents is a merge commit.

rules.text: Every object id is content-addressed: SHA = SHA-1(header + content), header = '<type> <byte-length>\0'. Same content always produces the same id anywhere, which is why blobs/trees dedupe automatically; git hash-object --stdin reproduces the id git itself would assign. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git Objects, 'Object Storage'.]

predicate.spec: an object's id equals SHA-1 of ('<type> <byte-length>\0' + content); git hash-object on the same content reproduces the same id git itself would assign.

rules.text: Objects are written zlib-compressed as loose objects under .git/objects/<2-hex>/<38-hex>; git gc rolls them into packfiles with delta compression once past a threshold (~7,000 loose objects or 50 packfiles by default, tunable via gc.auto/gc.autopacklimit). Packing is a storage-layer optimization only — it changes nothing about reachability or content addressing. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery, 'Maintenance'.] Footnote: Pro Git's prose rounds this to '~7,000 loose objects'; the git-gc/git-config reference docs give the exact gc.auto default as 6700 — same threshold, more precise number. [VERIFIED, git-gc docs and git-config docs, 'gc.auto'.]

A tag is a fourth object type. A lightweight tag is nothing but a ref (git update-ref refs/tags/<name> <sha>) pointing straight at a commit. An annotated tag (git tag -a) is a real tag OBJECT (tagger, date, message, one pointer to a commit) that the ref points at instead — only the annotated form carries metadata and can be signed. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git References, 'Tags'.]

predicate.spec: a lightweight tag is a bare ref pointing at a commit; an annotated tag is a distinct tag object (tagger+date+message+pointer to a commit) that the ref points at instead.

rules.text: .git/HEAD is normally a symbolic reference — literally 'ref: refs/heads/<branch>'. Checking out a tag, raw commit, or remote branch instead writes a raw SHA into HEAD ('detached HEAD' state), after which a new commit is one checkout away from becoming unreachable. Read/write HEAD safely via git symbolic-ref, not by hand outside refs/ syntax. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git References, 'The HEAD'.]

predicate.spec: HEAD is a symbolic ref to the current branch unless a tag/commit/remote-branch was checked out directly, in which case HEAD holds a raw commit SHA (detached HEAD).

rules.text: A branch is a plain file under refs/heads/<name> holding one commit SHA — a cheap, mutable pointer, not a copy of anything. git commit on a branch writes a new commit whose parent is the branch's current SHA, then advances the branch file — O(1) regardless of repo size. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git References, refs/heads layout.]

predicate.spec: a branch is a single file under refs/heads/<name> holding one commit SHA, updated in place by each commit on that branch.

rules.text: Refs (branches/tags/remotes) live as individual files under .git/refs/...; git gc consolidates them into .git/packed-refs (annotated-tag lines followed by a '^<peeled-sha>' line). Updating a packed ref writes a fresh loose file under refs/ rather than editing packed-refs in place; resolution checks the loose refs/ tree first, packed-refs as fallback. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery, 'Maintenance'.]

predicate.spec: refs are files under .git/refs/...; git gc may consolidate them into .git/packed-refs, and a loose ref file under refs/ always takes precedence over a packed-refs entry for the same name.

rules.text: The index ('staging area') is your proposed next commit — not itself a tree object but a flattened manifest of staged blob-SHA + path pairs (git ls-files -s shows it raw). git add updates it; git commit converts its current state into a tree via an internal write-tree and commits that tree. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Reset Demystified, 'The Index'.]

predicate.spec: the index is a flattened staged-blob/path manifest (not a tree object itself); git commit converts its current state into a tree via write-tree.

rules.text: git reset [--soft|--mixed|--hard] <target> rewrites up to three trees in strict order, stopping where told: (1) move HEAD's branch pointer — stop for --soft; (2) make the index match — the DEFAULT (--mixed) if no flag given; (3) make the working directory match the index — only for --hard, which discards uncommitted changes there. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Reset Demystified, 'Recap'; git-reset docs DISCUSSION table.]

predicate.spec: git reset --soft moves only the branch HEAD pointer; --mixed (default) also resets the index to match; --hard also overwrites the working directory to match the index.

rules.text: git merge <branch> fast-forwards (moves the pointer, no new commit) when the target's tip is a direct ancestor of the current tip. Otherwise it performs a three-way merge (default strategy 'ort', using the two tips + common ancestor) producing a new two-parent commit; with multiple common ancestors, ort merges them first as the reference tree, reducing spurious conflicts vs the older 'recursive' strategy. ort has been the default merge strategy only since Git 2.34 — recursive was the default for resolving two heads from Git v0.99.9k through v2.33.0 inclusive; a pre-2.34 git defaults to recursive instead. [VERIFIED, Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging; merge-strategies docs 'ort'/'recursive'.]

predicate.spec: git merge fast-forwards (moves the pointer, no new commit) when the target tip is an ancestor of the current tip; otherwise it performs a three-way merge producing a two-parent commit, using strategy ort by default since Git 2.34 (recursive was default from v0.99.9k through v2.33.0).

rules.text: A merge conflict pauses instead of committing: git status lists the file under 'Unmerged paths', and git writes <<<<<<< HEAD / ======= / >>>>>>> <branch> markers into the file. Resolve by editing to final content, removing markers, git add <file>, then git commit (or git merge --abort to cancel entirely). [VERIFIED, Git Branching - Basic Branching and Merging, 'Basic Merge Conflicts'.]

predicate.spec: a merge conflict leaves the file with <<<<<<<//=======//>>>>>>> markers and the path listed as unmerged in git status; resolving requires editing then git add before git commit (or git merge --abort to cancel).

rules.text: Do not let the merge strategy be an accident of which commands you typed. A fast-forward suits a straight-line personal extension nobody else built on; a real three-way merge commit suits integrating a completed, independently-meaningful line of work whose history is worth preserving. Forcing one shape onto the other discards true information about how the work happened.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was the choice between a fast-forward and an explicit three-way merge commit made deliberately based on whether the branch is a straight-line personal extension vs an independently-meaningful line of work to preserve, rather than defaulted to one shape for every merge?

rules.text: git rebase <upstream> locates the common ancestor of your branch and <upstream>, computes the patch each of your unique commits introduced, checks out <upstream>'s tip, and reapplies those patches one at a time — a brand-new commit (new SHA, new parent) each time, even for content-identical trees. [VERIFIED, Git Branching - Rebasing, 'The Basic Rebase'.]

predicate.spec: git rebase <upstream> finds the merge-base of the current branch and upstream, computes the patch for each of the branch's unique commits, and reapplies them in order on top of upstream's tip, producing new commit objects (new SHAs) even for identical content.

rules.text: THE GOLDEN RULE, verbatim: 'Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that people may have based work on.' Rebase abandons original commits and creates new-but-similar ones; rewriting and re-pushing already-pulled history forces every downstream collaborator to reconcile diverging histories by hand. [VERIFIED verbatim, Git Branching - Rebasing, 'The Perils of Rebasing'.]

predicate.spec: commits that exist outside the local repository and that others may have based work on are never rewritten by rebase (or any history-rewriting command) without explicit coordination.

rules.text: Merge and rebase trade off topological honesty against linear readability. Prefer merge to preserve the true shape of diverged/reunited history, especially once a branch is public (git-19 forbids rebasing it anyway). Prefer rebase on not-yet-shared local/feature-branch commits to fold in upstream cleanly and leave a bisect-friendly trail before sharing. Never rebase to simulate a merge that didn't happen; never merge-then-rebase-then-force-push a branch others already pulled.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is the merge-vs-rebase choice justified by whether the branch/commits are already shared (favor merge / git-19 forbids rebase) versus still local-only (rebase is fine to keep history linear), rather than a blanket preference for one over the other?

rules.text: git rebase -i <after-this-commit> opens a todo list, one 'pick <sha> <oneline>' line per commit AFTER that point, oldest-to-newest, excluding merge commits by default. The oneline text is cosmetic only — git tracks each entry by hash, not by that text. Reordering lines reorders replay; deleting a line drops the commit. [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, 'INTERACTIVE MODE'.]

predicate.spec: git rebase -i <after-this-commit> lists one 'pick <sha> <oneline>' line per commit after that point, oldest first, excluding merge commits by default; the oneline text is cosmetic and git tracks each entry by commit hash.

rules.text: Todo-list verbs: pick (keep as-is); reword (edit only the message); edit (pause after applying to amend content); squash (combine into previous, prompting to merge messages); fixup (combine into previous, DISCARD this message); drop (remove the commit). --continue/--skip/--abort control a paused sequence. [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, 'INTERACTIVE MODE'.]

predicate.spec: the interactive rebase todo verbs are pick (keep as-is), reword (edit message only), edit (pause to amend), squash (merge into previous, combine messages), fixup (merge into previous, discard this message), and drop (remove the commit).

rules.text: --autosquash automatically relocates commits whose message begins 'squash! ', 'fixup! ', or 'amend! ' next to the commit their remainder-of-title or hash matches, during interactive rebase; pair with git commit --fixup=<target>/--squash=<target> so cleanup needs zero manual reordering. [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, '--autosquash'.]

predicate.spec: --autosquash relocates commits whose message starts with 'squash! ', 'fixup! ', or 'amend! ' next to the commit their remainder-of-title or hash matches, during interactive rebase.

rules.text: --exec <cmd> appends an 'exec <cmd>' step after every commit the rebase produces (e.g. run tests after each replayed commit); any exec command exiting non-zero halts the rebase with exit code 1 at that point. Multiple --exec flags run in sequence; combined with --autosquash, exec runs once per squash/fixup series. [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, '--exec'.]

predicate.spec: --exec <cmd> appends an exec step after every commit rebase creates; if the command exits non-zero the rebase stops with exit code 1 at that point.

rules.text: --onto <newbase> transplants replayed commits onto an arbitrary commit instead of implicit <upstream>: (1) transplant a topic branch — git rebase --onto B A topic re-parents topic's unique commits as if forked from B; (2) rebase only part of a branch — git rebase --onto master topicA topicB moves just topicB's commits, leaving topicA untouched (also how a bad commit range is surgically removed). [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, 'TRANSPLANTING A TOPIC BRANCH WITH --ONTO'.]

predicate.spec: --onto <newbase> replays the commit range onto <newbase> instead of onto <upstream>, enabling transplanting a topic branch to a different base or rebasing only part of a branch (e.g. git rebase --onto master topicA topicB).

rules.text: Interactive rebase drops merge commits from the todo list by default, linearizing history. --rebase-merges regenerates label/reset/merge todo commands to recreate the same commit-graph topology on the new base, for when the branch structure itself is meaningful and must survive the rebase. [VERIFIED, git-rebase docs, 'REBASING MERGES'.]

predicate.spec: interactive rebase drops merge commits from the todo list by default (linearizing); --rebase-merges instead regenerates label/reset/merge todo commands to recreate the same branch/merge topology on the new base.

rules.text: git cherry-pick <commit>... applies the CHANGE each commit introduced onto the current branch as a new commit (new SHA, same content, current branch as parent). -x appends a '(cherry picked from commit <sha>)' trailer for traceability; -n/--no-commit applies without committing, for combining several picks into one. [VERIFIED, git-cherry-pick docs, SYNOPSIS + -x/-n.]

predicate.spec: git cherry-pick <commit> applies that commit's change as a new commit (new SHA) on the current branch; -x appends a 'cherry picked from commit <sha>' trailer, -n/--no-commit applies without committing.

rules.text: A cherry-pick over multiple commits that hits a conflict pauses the sequence: resolve + git add, then --continue; or --skip the offending commit; or --abort to cancel back to the pre-sequence state; or --quit to clear sequencer state without rewinding. [VERIFIED, git-cherry-pick docs, 'SEQUENCER SUBCOMMANDS'.]

predicate.spec: a multi-commit cherry-pick that conflicts pauses; --continue resumes after resolving+adding, --skip skips the current commit, --abort cancels back to the pre-sequence state, --quit clears sequencer state without rewinding.

rules.text: git stash push snapshots working-tree + index changes vs HEAD into a stash entry, then rolls the working tree and index back to HEAD. By default excludes untracked/ignored files — pass -u/--include-untracked to include untracked, -a/--all to also include ignored. Omitting 'push' is a supported quick-snapshot shorthand. [VERIFIED, git-stash docs, 'COMMANDS' push.]

predicate.spec: git stash push snapshots working-tree+index changes vs HEAD into a stash entry and resets working tree/index to HEAD; untracked files are excluded unless -u/--include-untracked, ignored files excluded unless -a/--all.

rules.text: git stash list/show inspect entries. git stash apply reapplies and LEAVES the entry (use when you might need it again); git stash pop reapplies then DROPS it. git stash branch <name> [<stash>] creates a fresh branch from a stash — the safest reapply when the target has diverged enough to conflict. [VERIFIED, git-stash docs, SYNOPSIS + apply/pop/branch.]

predicate.spec: git stash list/show inspect entries; apply reapplies and keeps the entry, pop reapplies and drops it, and stash branch <name> creates a branch from a stash for conflicted reapplies.

rules.text: The latest stash you created is stored in refs/stash; older stashes are found in the reflog of this reference and can be named via the usual reflog syntax (stash@{0} most recent, stash@{1} before it, stash@{2.hours.ago} also works). [VERIFIED, git-stash docs, DESCRIPTION.] In other words a stash entry is backed by ordinary commit object(s) reachable through that ref/reflog, not a separate magical storage class [INFERRED]. Treat git stash drop and especially git stash clear with the same caution as deleting a branch: content is gc-eligible once unreferenced, recoverable only through the same reflog/fsck techniques (§10), within the local reflog's retention window.

git worktree add <path> [<commit-ish>] creates an additional linked working tree sharing the same repository/object store as the existing checkout, but with its own working directory, HEAD, and index — enabling two branches checked out SIMULTANEOUSLY without a second clone. If <commit-ish> is a matching single-remote tracking branch, or omitted, git infers a sensible branch to create/checkout. [VERIFIED, git-worktree docs, DESCRIPTION + add.]

predicate.spec: git worktree add <path> [<commit-ish>] creates a linked working tree sharing the repository's object store but with its own working directory, HEAD, and index, allowing two branches checked out simultaneously.

rules.text: A repository has exactly one main worktree (from init/clone) and zero-or-more linked worktrees. The main worktree can NEVER be removed via git worktree remove. git worktree list [--porcelain] enumerates all worktrees with path/HEAD/branch state. [VERIFIED, git-worktree docs, DESCRIPTION + remove.]

predicate.spec: a repository has exactly one main worktree (from init/clone) which git worktree remove can never remove, plus zero or more linked worktrees enumerable via git worktree list.

rules.text: git worktree remove only succeeds on a CLEAN linked worktree (no untracked/modified files); a dirty one, or one containing submodules, needs --force. git worktree prune cleans up metadata left behind when a worktree directory was deleted manually (not via remove). git worktree lock/unlock protects a worktree from being pruned or moved. [VERIFIED, git-worktree docs, COMMANDS remove/prune/lock.]

predicate.spec: git worktree remove only succeeds on a clean linked worktree (or with --force for dirty/submodule-containing ones); worktree prune cleans up metadata for manually-deleted worktree directories; lock/unlock protects a worktree from pruning/moving.

rules.text: If the main repo or a linked worktree directory is moved by hand (plain mv, not git worktree move), the administrative links break. git worktree repair [<path>...] run from the main worktree (or the moved worktree, or given each new path) reestablishes the bidirectional pointers. [VERIFIED, git-worktree docs, 'repair'.]

predicate.spec: after a main repo or linked worktree directory is moved by hand (not via worktree move), git worktree repair [<path>...] reestablishes the broken administrative links between them.

rules.text: git bisect start, then mark one bad (git bisect bad [<rev>], default HEAD) and at least one good (git bisect good <rev>) commit. Git checks out the midpoint of the remaining range; classify it good/bad/skip repeatedly. Range halves each time — O(log n) steps to isolate the first bad commit, left checked out and recorded at refs/bisect/bad. [VERIFIED, git-bisect docs, 'Basic bisect commands: start, bad, good'.]

predicate.spec: git bisect start plus one bad and at least one good revision begins a binary search: each step checks out the midpoint, you classify it good/bad/skip, and the range halves until the first bad commit is isolated in O(log n) steps.

rules.text: git bisect run <cmd> [<args>] fully automates the loop using the script's exit code: exit 0 = good, exit code between 1 and 127 inclusive EXCEPT 125 = bad, exit 125 = untestable (auto-skip, see bisect skip), and any OTHER exit code aborts the bisect process entirely (not treated as good/bad/skip). --term-bad=<word>/--term-good=<word> (e.g. new/old) replace the good/bad vocabulary when 'bad' is semantically backwards (bisecting when a fix was introduced). [VERIFIED, git-bisect docs, 'Bisect run' + --term-*.]

predicate.spec: git bisect run <cmd> automates the good/bad loop using the command's exit code: 0=good; 1-127 inclusive except 125=bad; 125=untestable/skip (auto git bisect skip); any other exit code aborts the bisect process entirely. --term-bad/--term-good rename the good/bad vocabulary.

rules.text: git bisect reset ends the session, returning to the pre-bisect branch/commit (do this even after finding the answer — bisect otherwise leaves a detached HEAD, git-10). git bisect log records the session transcript; git bisect replay <logfile> reruns a previously logged session, for resuming later or handing off. [VERIFIED, git-bisect docs, SYNOPSIS + reset/log/replay.]

predicate.spec: git bisect reset ends the session and returns to the pre-bisect checkout; git bisect log records the session and git bisect replay <logfile> reruns a previously logged session.

rules.text: Every local ref update (commit, checkout, reset, rebase, merge, branch/tag create/delete) is appended to a per-ref log under .git/logs/<ref> (plus .git/logs/HEAD), readable via git reflog [show] [<ref>] as <ref>@{N} entries. Entries expire on a schedule: gc.reflogExpire (default 90 days, reachable-from-tip) and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (default 30 days, unreachable) — after which git gc may delete the underlying objects. [VERIFIED, git-reflog docs, 'Options for expire'.]

predicate.spec: every local ref update is appended to a per-ref reflog under .git/logs/, readable via git reflog show <ref>; entries expire per gc.reflogExpire (default 90 days, reachable) and gc.reflogExpireUnreachable (default 30 days, unreachable).

rules.text: RECOVERY RECIPE: to recover from an over-eager reset --hard, accidental branch delete, or a rebase/amend regretted — run git reflog (or git reflog show <old-branch-name> if the reflog file survived the deletion) to find the pre-mistake SHA, then git branch <new-name> <sha> to recover it under a new name, or git reset --hard <sha> to snap the current branch straight back. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery, 'Data Recovery'.]

predicate.spec: recovering from an unwanted reset/rebase/branch-delete: locate the pre-mistake SHA via git reflog (or git reflog show <old-branch>), then git branch <new> <sha> or git reset --hard <sha> to restore it.

rules.text: LAST RESORT: if the reflog entry itself is gone, run git fsck --full, which lists every object not pointed to by any other object as 'dangling commit <sha>'/'dangling blob <sha>'/etc. A dangling commit is intact data with no ref keeping it alive; recover it the same way as git-40, by pointing a new branch at its SHA — do this before running git gc, which reclaims genuinely unreachable objects. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery, 'Data Recovery'.]

predicate.spec: when no reflog entry remains, git fsck --full lists dangling commit/blob/tree objects unreachable from any ref; a dangling commit is recovered by pointing a new branch at its SHA, done before running git gc.

rules.text: The full recovery stack, in order: (1) still reachable from a ref? plain git log/git branch suffices. (2) in a reflog? git reflog (git-40). (3) dangling with no reflog left? git fsck --full (git-41). (4) none of those find it → genuinely gone (never committed, or fell outside both expiry windows and was gc'd). The whole stack is local to one clone — it recovers nothing that only ever existed on a machine you don't have.

git gc --auto is the mechanism bounding the recovery window above: it does nothing until ~7,000 loose objects or 50 packfiles accumulate (gc.auto/gc.autopacklimit; footnote — the git-gc/git-config docs give the exact gc.auto default as 6700, see git-8), at which point it packs/prunes past-expiry objects and rolls per-file refs into .git/packed-refs (git-12). An explicit git gc can run this immediately and shrink the recovery window on demand — don't run it reflexively on a repo where git-41 might still be needed. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Maintenance and Data Recovery, 'Maintenance'.]

predicate.spec: git gc --auto only performs a real collection past roughly 7,000 loose objects (exact gc.auto default: 6700) or 50 packfiles (tunable via gc.auto/gc.autopacklimit); an explicit git gc can run immediately and shrink the recovery window (git-39..41) on demand.

rules.text: A submodule is a special 'gitlink' tree entry (a pinned commit SHA, not content) in the superproject, plus a path/URL/branch entry in a top-level .gitmodules file. Cloning/pulling a superproject creates the submodule directory EMPTY: git submodule init (registers config) AND git submodule update (fetches + checks out the pinned commit) are both required, or clone with --recurse-submodules. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Submodules, 'Cloning a Project with Submodules'.]

predicate.spec: a submodule is a gitlink tree entry (pinned commit SHA) in the superproject plus a path/url/branch entry in .gitmodules; a plain clone/pull leaves the submodule directory empty until git submodule init && update (or --recurse-submodules).

rules.text: git submodule foreach '<cmd>' runs an arbitrary shell command inside EVERY submodule in turn (e.g. git stash, or git checkout -b featureA) — the standard way to batch an operation across submodules instead of cd-ing into each by hand. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Submodules, 'Submodule Foreach'.]

predicate.spec: git submodule foreach '<cmd>' runs the given command inside every submodule in turn.

rules.text: git pull on the superproject recursively FETCHES submodule commits by default but does NOT update the submodule's checked-out working copy. git status reports the submodule path as 'modified... new commits' until git submodule update runs explicitly — fetch and checkout are two separate acts for submodules. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Submodules, 'Pulling Upstream Changes from the Project Remote'.]

predicate.spec: git pull on the superproject recursively fetches submodule commits by default but does not update the submodule's checked-out working copy; git status reports it modified with new commits until git submodule update runs.

rules.text: Treat every submodule pointer bump as a deliberate, reviewed commit — it pins an exact SHA everyone updating will receive, so an accidental bump (e.g. from `update --remote` run without checking the diff) is an uncontrolled dependency upgrade. A submodule checked out at its pin is normally in detached HEAD (git-10); real work inside it needs its own branch first, or it risks becoming unreachable (git-42) once the pin moves.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is a submodule pointer bump reviewed as a deliberate pinned-dependency change (not an incidental side effect of `update --remote`), and is work inside the submodule done on an actual branch rather than left on its default detached HEAD?

rules.text: A hook is an executable script under .git/hooks/, named EXACTLY after the event (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, pre-receive...) with NO extension. git init/clone seed the directory with '<name>.sample' examples; activating one means renaming to drop '.sample' and making it executable (chmod +x) — any language works via its shebang. [VERIFIED, Customizing Git - Git Hooks, 'Installing a Hook'.]

predicate.spec: a hook is an executable file under .git/hooks/ named exactly after the event with no extension; the .sample templates git seeds must be renamed (dropping .sample) and made executable to activate.

rules.text: Client-side hooks are NEVER copied when a repository is cloned — they live only in that one local .git/hooks/. A policy that must hold for every contributor cannot rely on a client-side hook being present; it belongs on the server side (git-50) or in CI. [VERIFIED, Customizing Git - Git Hooks, 'Client-Side Hooks' note.]

predicate.spec: client-side hook files under .git/hooks/ are never transferred by git clone; a policy that must hold for every contributor cannot rely on a client-side hook being present.

rules.text: Server-side pre-receive runs once per push, receiving every pushed ref on stdin BEFORE any is accepted; a non-zero exit rejects the ENTIRE push — the right place for access control / fast-forward-only policy. post-receive runs only AFTER acceptance (notifications/CI/ticket updates) and CANNOT reject or unwind the push; the client stays connected until it finishes, so keep it fast. [VERIFIED, Customizing Git - Git Hooks, 'pre-receive'/'post-receive'.]

predicate.spec: server-side pre-receive receives all pushed refs before any are accepted and a non-zero exit rejects the entire push; post-receive runs only after acceptance and cannot reject or undo the push.

rules.text: [INFERRED] Because client-side hooks aren't cloned (git-49), a team wanting shared, versioned hook behavior points core.hooksPath at a repo-tracked directory instead of the untracked .git/hooks/, with contributors opting in (or a bootstrap step setting it) after cloning.

predicate.spec: pointing core.hooksPath at a repo-tracked directory lets a team version and share hook scripts despite git-49's per-clone hook storage.

rules.text: Setting the text attribute enables end-of-line normalization: on add/commit, endings normalize to LF IN THE INDEX regardless of working-tree ending; on checkout, eol (or core.autocrlf/core.eol if eol is unset — default CRLF on Windows, LF elsewhere) decides what the working copy gets back. text=auto lets git guess binary-vs-text. Get this right BEFORE the first mixed-ending commit — retrofitting rewrites history. [VERIFIED, gitattributes docs, 'text'/'eol'.]

predicate.spec: the text attribute normalizes a path's line endings to LF in the index on checkin regardless of working-tree ending; eol (or core.autocrlf/core.eol if eol is unset) controls whether checkout writes LF or CRLF.

rules.text: export-ignore excludes a path from git archive output (e.g. drop tests/CI config from a release tarball without deleting them from the repo). A custom merge driver is declared in .git/config/~/.gitconfig under [merge "<name>"] with a driver command template (%O/%A/%B ancestor/ours/theirs temp files, %L conflict-marker length), opted into per-path via '<pattern> merge=<name>' in .gitattributes. [VERIFIED, gitattributes docs, 'export-ignore' + 'Defining a custom merge driver'.]

predicate.spec: export-ignore excludes a path from git archive output; a custom merge driver is declared under [merge "<name>"] with a driver command template using %O/%A/%B/%L and applied per-path via '<pattern> merge=<name>' in .gitattributes.

rules.text: conflict-marker-size=<N> on a path lengthens the <<<<<<</=======/>>>>>>> markers from the 7-character default to N — needed for files whose content can itself contain 7 leading <, =, or > characters (nested diffs, some markup) where the default width would be ambiguous. [VERIFIED, gitattributes docs, 'conflict-marker-size'.]

predicate.spec: the conflict-marker-size=<N> attribute lengthens conflict markers from the 7-character default to N characters for a matched path.

rules.text: Ignore-pattern precedence, HIGHEST to LOWEST (last matching line wins within one source): command-line patterns > .gitignore in the same/parent directory (closer overrides farther) > $GIT_COMMON_DIR/info/exclude (local, unshared) > core.excludesFile (global, unshared). Shared patterns belong in a versioned .gitignore; purely personal ignores belong in info/exclude or core.excludesFile. [VERIFIED, gitignore docs, 'DESCRIPTION' precedence list.]

predicate.spec: ignore-pattern precedence highest-to-lowest is: command-line patterns > nearest .gitignore file (closer overrides farther) > $GIT_COMMON_DIR/info/exclude > core.excludesFile, with the last matching line winning within one source.

rules.text: A leading ! negates a pattern, re-including a file an earlier pattern excluded — EXCEPT you cannot re-include a file whose PARENT DIRECTORY is itself excluded: git doesn't descend into an excluded directory to evaluate patterns for files inside it (performance), so a ! targeting such a file silently has no effect. [VERIFIED, gitignore docs, 'PATTERN FORMAT'.]

predicate.spec: a leading ! re-includes a file excluded by an earlier pattern, except when the file's parent directory is itself excluded, in which case git does not descend to re-evaluate it.

rules.text: .gitignore only governs UNTRACKED files. A path already git-added/committed keeps being tracked and keeps showing in status/diffs no matter what pattern is added afterward — stop tracking it first with git rm --cached <path> (leaves the file on disk) before the ignore pattern takes effect. [VERIFIED, gitignore docs, 'DESCRIPTION', 'Files already tracked by Git are not affected'.]

predicate.spec: gitignore patterns never stop an already-tracked file from being tracked/shown; git rm --cached <path> must remove it from tracking first.

rules.text: Configure user.signingkey to your GPG key id (gpg --list-keys / --gen-key first), then git commit -S signs a commit and git tag -s <name> signs a tag at creation. Verify with git tag -v <name> (or git log --show-signature): success prints 'gpg: Good signature from...'; without the signer's public key you get 'public key not found'. [VERIFIED, Git Tools - Signing Your Work, 'GPG Introduction' + 'Verifying Tags'.]

predicate.spec: user.signingkey plus git commit -S / git tag -s produce a signature; git tag -v (or git log --show-signature) verifies it, reporting 'Good signature' or a public-key-not-found error.

rules.text: Only an ANNOTATED tag can carry a signature, because only the annotated form is a real tag OBJECT (tagger+date+message+pointer, git-9) — a lightweight tag is nothing but a ref, with no object to attach a signature to. -s (or -a plus a manual signature) is a prerequisite for any tag-verification workflow. [VERIFIED, Git Internals - Git References, 'Tags'.]

predicate.spec: only an annotated tag (a real tag object) can carry a signature; a lightweight tag, being only a ref, has no object to sign.

rules.text: Require signed commits/tags at release boundaries and for any externally-consumed artifact (a published release tag, a hotfix cherry-picked into a support branch) as the actual proof of provenance — an unsigned annotated tag is still just a movable-in-spirit label anyone with push access could recreate; a verified signature is what turns 'this tag says v2.0' into 'a specific known identity attested to this exact commit as v2.0.'
rules.reviewer_criterion: Are signed commits/tags required at release boundaries and for externally-consumed artifacts, so that a published tag's authenticity is backed by a verifiable identity rather than only by push access?

rules.text: [INFERRED, standard practitioner convention] Shape each commit as one coherent, independently buildable/testable change with an imperative-mood summary line ('Add X', not 'Added X'/'Adds X'), and use interactive rebase (§5: squash/fixup/reword/drop) to fold exploratory/typo-fix/oops commits into their logical parent BEFORE the branch is shared — so git log and git bisect (§9) read as deliberate engineering steps and a bisect never lands on a commit that doesn't build.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Is each commit shaped as one coherent, buildable change with an imperative-mood summary, with exploratory/fixup commits folded in via interactive rebase before the branch is shared, so log/bisect read as deliberate steps?

rules.text: When a pushed branch needs pushing again after a local rewrite, prefer git push --force-with-lease over bare --force. --force disables ALL safety checks and unconditionally overwrites the remote ref — including any commits a collaborator pushed since your last fetch, silently discarding their work. --force-with-lease[=<ref>:<expected-sha>] only proceeds if the remote ref still points where you last saw it; otherwise it fails loudly instead of overwriting. [VERIFIED, git-push docs, '--force-with-lease' + '--force'.]

predicate.spec: pushing a rewritten branch uses --force-with-lease (fails if the remote ref has moved since last seen) rather than bare --force (unconditionally overwrites the remote, including others' unfetched pushes).

rules.text: On an already-public/shared branch, prefer git revert <commit> over any history rewrite to undo it: revert adds a NEW commit that inverses the change, leaving the original commit and rest of history intact — safe to push normally (no force, no golden-rule violation per git-19) and requiring no coordination with anyone who already has the original commit. Reserve rebase-based rewriting (§4-§5, plus git-62 discipline) for history that is still effectively yours alone.
rules.reviewer_criterion: On an already-shared/public branch, is git revert used to undo a change (adding an inverse commit) rather than any history-rewriting approach, reserving rewrites for still-local, not-yet-shared history?
